title: Password Cracking Cost
description: Interactive p5.js calculator showing how the choice of password hash (raw SHA-256, salt, bcrypt, Argon2id), attacker hardware, and database size change the time and dollar cost to crack a stolen password database.
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: cybersecurity

educational.topic: Password storage, salting, and slow/memory-hard hashing
learningObjectives: Analyze how each password-protection technique changes the attacker's effective guess rate.
Compare the time and dollar cost to crack a stolen database across hardware tiers and hash functions.
Recognize raw SHA-256 (with or without salt) as an insecure choice for password storage.
educational.prerequisites: Knowledge that passwords are stored as hashes; basic idea of a hash function.

pedagogical.assessment: Discussion questions in the lesson plan ask students to find the cheapest secure configuration and reason about rainbow tables.
misconceptionsAddressed: Believing a strong hash like SHA-256 is appropriate for password storage.
Thinking salt alone makes passwords safe (it stops rainbow tables but not fast brute force).
Underestimating how memory-hardness neutralizes GPU/ASIC parallelism.

model.assumptions: Hardware guess rates and hash work-factors are hard-coded order-of-magnitude figures calibrated against published 2025 GPU benchmarks; about 25% of accounts assumed crackable within a ~1e9-guess budget.
model.limitations: A teaching model, not a precise cracking simulator. Real costs depend on password-policy strength, wordlist quality, GPU spot pricing, and hash parameters.
